name: Yusuf Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Normal day is a night, for me. I do ten till six at the 24-hour Brightmart on the ring road, so I'm on the till till about two, then I'm filling shelves, mostly tins and pet food, while the floor polisher goes round. I like the regulars who come in at midnight, the taxi drivers and the nurses off shift, because they actually talk to you. What wears me out is the self-checkouts beeping all night and me running between them for every bag of loose onions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years now, since I was twenty. I share a flat with my cousin Dani above a takeaway on Mill Street, and rent eats about half my pay. I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank on a good month, and there's only Brightmart and one small discount shop anywhere I can get to without a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now they'll stop telling us the machines are coming for us every other week. At work I'd say it in the canteen to Pat, who's been on tills thirty years and is sick of hearing it. Online I don't really post, but I'd share something from the union page saying the scare was a way to keep us quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, because my problem was never AI. My supermarket already went from ten staffed tills to four at night when they put in twelve self-checkouts last year. That was plain machines, not clever ones, and they still cut our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights, because that's the only shift with the extra pay on top. I'd go to the union meeting at the library in January and push for a deal on minimum hours. And I'd try again to put twenty a week aside, though that never lasts past the first broken thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's the same old squeeze. Rent went up again in September and the pay rise was pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your problem was never AI. If nothing big changes, what is the thing that would knock you over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler, or my hours getting cut again. If Brightmart takes another four hours off my week, I'm short on rent, simple as that. Even with no clever robots, the self-checkouts are still there and the managers still count heads every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani covers me sometimes and I cover him, that's how we've always done it. The union rep, Carol, fought for Pat when they tried to move her to days. Past that there isn't really anyone, my mum's got her own bills.

say: The AI scare was mostly a **story to scare staff** into accepting less.
Pat and I are still needed, so the **union** should push for **guaranteed hours** now.
think: The **self-checkouts** already took our night tills, and that has nothing to do with clever AI.
My real risk is a **cut in hours** that leaves me short on **rent**.
do: **Keep** the night shift because the **extra night pay** is what keeps rent covered.
Go to the **union meeting** in January and push for **minimum hours**.
Try to put **twenty a week** aside before something breaks again.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, worn down by **rent rises** and tiny pay rises.
S0.quote: My supermarket already went from ten staffed tills to four at night when they put in twelve self-checkouts last year.
fieldNote: He separates **AI** from the **self-checkouts** that already cut his night shift.
His **thin savings** and one-wage rent mean any hours cut is an immediate crisis.
Leans on **cousin Dani** and the union, with almost no other safety net.

steps.text: Keep the Brightmart night shift for the extra night pay
Push for minimum guaranteed hours at the January union meeting
Put twenty a week into savings before the boiler breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is bosses using software to squeeze more out of fewer people. At work I'd tell the younger lads to join the union before the cuts, not after. Online I'd share the petitions about keeping a staffed till in every shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the ordering and the rota already run on a computer, so the people they'll cut first are the supervisors and the office girl, Joanne. Then they'll look at the shop floor once the shelf robots get cheaper. I'm hands-on, so I've got longer, but in a place with two shops, longer isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every hour I can now, take the extra Sunday shifts, and stop buying lunch from the takeaway. I'd get Carol to put my name down as a union contact for nights. I'm not going on any AI course, I'd be useless and I'd rather spend the time on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm standing on a beach watching the water come in slowly. You know it's coming, you just don't know which wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never go on an AI course. If Brightmart offered one, paid, would you still say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid, I'd go, because I'm not daft. But I'd sit at the back and I don't think it would stick. Phones and apps just don't go in my head, I've tried with the rota app and my cousin Dani still has to do my swaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, honestly. She's fifty-eight and she's never done anything but tills, so where does she go? If they push her out, I'll be at that meeting shouting.

say: This is **bosses** using software to do more with **fewer people**.
Young staff should **join the union** before the **cuts** start, not after.
think: The **office jobs** like ordering and rotas go first, then robots come for the **shop floor**.
Being hands-on buys him a little time, but in a **two-shop area** that's not much.
do: **Take** extra Sunday shifts and stop buying **takeaway lunches**.
Become the **night-shift union contact** through Carol, the store rep.
Refuse a self-paid **AI course**, but attend one if Brightmart **pays** for it.
feel: **Dread** that builds slowly, like watching the **tide** come in.
**Protective anger** on behalf of older colleagues like Pat.
S1.quote: Phones and apps just don't go in my head, I've tried with the rota app and my cousin Dani still has to do my swaps.
fieldNote: He sees the **office side** of retail going first and the floor later.
Admits he would attend **paid training** but doubts it would stick.
His anger is **collective**: he worries more about Pat than about himself.

steps.text: Take every extra Sunday shift Brightmart offers
Stop buying lunch from the takeaway downstairs
Sign up as the union contact for the night shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in today, not in a report next year. I'd be at any protest in town, and I'd be the one telling people in the canteen that this needs a law, not a shrug. If shops don't need us, they should pay tax for every machine that replaces us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished at Brightmart by 2031, and maybe sooner on the till side. The thinking AI does the ordering and the rota straight away in 2028, and then three years later the shelf-filling robot turns up and I've got nothing left. I've no skills on paper except seven years of beeping things through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop pretending I can save and just keep the rent paid. I'd sign up with the union campaign the first week and get Dani and me onto a cheaper flat list. If it came, I'd ask about benefits straight away instead of being too proud, because two weeks of money goes nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. There's no time to learn anything and nowhere to go even if I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have about three years between the thinking AI in 2028 and the robots in 2031. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every hour going and hold on. I know I should train for something, but what, when the thinking jobs are already gone? Maybe care work, my auntie does it and robots won't be washing old people that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dani the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in this together and we're not losing the flat. Then I'd probably sit up all night doing sums that don't add up.

say: The government must **act now** and pass a **law** to protect shop workers.
Shops should pay **tax** for every machine that replaces a worker.
think: He expects to be **finished at Brightmart** by 2031, with tills going even sooner.
Seven years on tills gives him **nothing on paper** to take elsewhere.
do: **Join** the union campaign in the first week of the announcement.
Put his and Dani's names on a **cheaper flat** list.
Apply for **benefits** quickly instead of waiting until the money runs out.
feel: **Sick** and unsteady, like the floor has gone from under him.
**Trapped**, with no time to learn and nowhere local to go.
S2.quote: I've no skills on paper except seven years of beeping things through.
fieldNote: The two-year warning leaves him with **no plan** and no money to make one.
He grasps the **three-year gap** but cannot see what to train for.
**Care work**, via his auntie, is the only escape he names.

steps.text: Join the union campaign in the first week
Get on the list for a cheaper flat with Dani
Apply for benefits as soon as hours are cut
Work every Brightmart hour going until the robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say we need laws, but I'd also say we've got five years, so let's use them properly. I'd push the union to get the company to pay for retraining before the robots come in 2034. People would listen more if there was a plan and not just shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for clever people and not enough for me. I'd still drift along until something forced my hand. That's how I am, I stayed seven years in one job because changing scares me more than staying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask my auntie properly about care work, maybe do a weekend shift with her agency to see if I can stand it. I'd keep nights at Brightmart because that's the rent. And I'd go to the union every month, not just when there's trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the two-year one, but heavy. It's like being told the date of an exam I know I'll fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said changing scares you more than staying. What is it about changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being new and slow again, with everyone watching. On the till I know where everything is and I'm good with the drunk lot at 3am. In a new job I'm just the bloke who doesn't know where the gloves are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If care work didn't suit you, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know, and I'm being honest. There's a warehouse out past the bypass but that's robots too by then. I'd probably just stay until they close the door on me.

say: Five years means the **union** must get the company to **pay for retraining**.
A clear **plan** wins more support than **shouting** at the bosses.
think: Five years is enough for clever people but **not for him**, he admits.
He fears being **new and slow** again more than he fears staying put.
do: **Try** a weekend shift with his auntie's **care agency** this first year.
**Keep** the Brightmart nights because they pay the **rent**.
Go to **union meetings** every month, not only when trouble starts.
feel: **Heavy** and resigned, like waiting for an **exam** he expects to fail.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for clever people and not enough for me.
fieldNote: The extra time eases panic but not **his outlook** on himself.
He names **fear of being new** as the real block to retraining.
Without care work he expects to **stay until closure**.

steps.text: Try a weekend shift with his auntie's care agency
Keep the Brightmart night shift to cover rent
Attend the union meeting every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently, so no excuses for the government or Brightmart. Train people, keep a staffed till by law, tax the machines. I'd say that to anyone at the bus stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'll be thirty-seven when the robots come for the shelves in 2039. That's young enough to do something else, which is almost worse, because I'll have no excuse. I think I'd still leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do nothing new, if I'm honest, apart from keeping up the union. Maybe in a few years I'd do the care certificate my auntie keeps going on about. I'd try to get Dani and me into a council flat list so the rent isn't half my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it nags at me. Ten years feels like forever until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing new this year. What would it take to get you started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone sitting me down and saying here's the course, it's Tuesdays, it's free, and you keep your shifts. If I've got to find it myself on a website, I won't. That's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your life looks like at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be in a job where people still need a person, maybe care, maybe something with the council. With my own flat, not a shared one. I don't want to end up like my workmate Pat at fifty-eight, hoping they forget she's there.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuses**: train people and keep a **staffed till** by law.
The government should **tax machines** that take shop jobs.
think: At **thirty-seven** he'll still be young enough to change, so he'll have no excuse.
He suspects he'll still **leave it too late**.
do: Keep going to the **union** while changing nothing else this year.
Consider the **care certificate** his auntie recommends in a few years.
Join the **council flat** list so rent is no longer half his pay.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, but the date keeps **nagging** at him.
S4.quote: I don't want to end up like my workmate Pat at fifty-eight, hoping they forget she's there.
fieldNote: The decade lowers urgency, but he openly predicts his own **delay**.
He needs training **handed to him**, free and around his shifts.
Still alarmed: he expects to lose the job, only **later**.

steps.text: Hold off on any new course for the first year
Keep attending union meetings at the library
Join the council flat list with his cousin Dani

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one in 2028, no question, because there's no time and I've got no money to buy time. What would help is a course I'm put on, free, on my days off, and a law that says a shop keeps people on the tills. And rent that isn't half of everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money when the robots do my job. Somebody's going to get richer off my seven years of nights, and it won't be me.

headlineQuote: Somebody's going to get richer off my seven years of nights, and it won't be me.
portrait: Yusuf, 27, has worked **nights** on the tills at Brightmart for seven years and shares a flat with his cousin.
**Rent** takes half his pay and he has about **two weeks** of savings.
He distrusts new tech, never uses AI, and puts his faith in the **union** and new laws.
He moves from **anxious** in the quiet worlds to **panicked** when AGI arrives in 2028.
He admits he would **wait too long** unless training was handed to him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there is no time and no **money** to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: A **free course** on his days off and a law keeping **staffed tills**.
**Lower rent**, so housing stops taking half of his pay.
